New York
January 25, 1954
Dear Familys
Just back from my 31st crossing of the Atlantic and thought you might be
interested in some of the highlights of this safari. On the 17th received a cable
from Germany that a deal which I have been concerned with for some years might go
through or fall through, dependent on whether I came over. That was attaching more
importance than warranted, but nevertheless with a great deal of regret I cancelled
out my participation in a weekend trip which Hebe and Frank had planned to Great
Barrington and got myself booked on the President Special, Friday the 15th.
Couldn't 'phone Debby so hen she thought I was on a trip to Massachusetts I was
in fact out over the Atlantic. It was the fastest trip I've made - only 10 1/2
hours from New York to London. The President Sp cial is an experiment of PAA's in
surcharged luxury: Meals by Maxim's of Paris, a red carpet out to the airplane, four
stewardesses - count 'em, four - orchids for the ladies, champagne but good and berths
for about half the passengers, with "sleeperette" chairs that lie almost flat for the
rest.
I met an old friend from Manila days, and after we took off at 4830 P.M. we
talked until dinner. After dinner we adjourned to the lower deck lounge and yak-
yakked until midnight, New York time. Then I realized that werd be in London at 3:00
A. Mo, New York time and he had bought a $25.00 berth, so chased him to bed. We had
a couple of hours sleep and then they called us for breakfast at 2800 A.M., New York
but 7:00 A.M. London time. That's one bad feature about a quick trip eastbound - you
don't get any sleep!
At London I transferred to a British European Airways Elizabethan Class twin-
engined plane for Amsterdam and Hamburg. The "Elizabethan" part was no doubt correct
but the "Class" was distinctly lacking. The interior looked like a cross between a
barn and a hen house. A single stewardess devoted her full attention to selling
cigarettes, beer and hard liquor. The lunch was typically British - cold and unin-

viting with a nasty "sweet" of cerise jello smeared neatly on top with a bit of whipped
cream, the wholeshivering mess encased in a greasy paper cup with thumb marks. It was a
marked contrast to the svelte elegance of the President Special, and unlike the latter
awfully easy to diet.
Arrived Hamburg in a heavy rain Saturday afternoon. Went to bed early that
night but couldn't sleep for four or five hours and woke up Sunday at what I thought
was 7:00 A.M. but turned out to be 1:00 P.M. which, after all, considering the six
hours difference in time was, in fact, 7800 A.M., New Iork time. I Just can't make my
old carcass conform to the clock!

Monday we caught a train at 7:00 A.M. for the Journey down to Dusseldorf -

must confess that I was just as scared as he would have been in the air, forthe train

hotel erected where an old one had been completely wrecked by bombs. Tuesday I

Rolshoven, who as you might suspedt is German, for a call on the reorganized Luft
Hansa. They are realy in trouble. 'They have airplanes ordered ready for delivery
but until something is done about the peace treaty they cant fly. They're all
dressed up and have nowhere to go!
On Wednesday I drove to Wiesbaden - then to Frankfurt to talk to thepa

lawyer - then back to Wiesbaden for the night with a letter of agreement dram up.
Thursday morning we signed the agreement and that afternoon I caught the PAA Clipper
to London. Sorry to be so cagey about my business deal but it is still "restricted"
as the Army says. However, it turned out better than I had hoped and quite an im
provement over what I had been authorized to sign, so feel all right about it •
Stopped off in London for a day to see our people there and left Friday
night for New York. There were storms out over our regular track across the North
Atlantic, so we were routed via Iceland. That was really a break for me because
Iceland was new territory - in fact about the only country I haven't visited before.
We flew over the capital city of Reykjavik in bright moonlight and it was almost 11ke
daylight. Landed at the Keflavik Airport in strange and unexpected contrast with a
snow-covered Idlewild Airport at New Iork where me took off between banks of snow on
either side of the runway; the fields of Europe were as green as mid-gummer and even
in Iceland there was no snow. Furthermore, it was a lot warmer than New Iork. We re-
fueled and then flew direct to New York. As in the case of my flight over, it was as
smooth as glass except over the tip of Greenland where we ran into a little turbulence.
Arrived in New York one minute ahead of schedule.
The Germans I talked to were mostly industrialists and bankers. None thought
that aything would come of the Four Power discussions in Berlin. They all agreed that
1f a really free election was held in East Germany the Communists wouldn't get enough
votes to fill a hat. In these circumstances the Russians are not likely to approve
any election except one of those Red "free elections" where they get all the votes.
However, It must be remembered that the Russians are unpredictable. In the recent
West German election the voters were as free as in the U.S. and the Commies failed to
win a single contest. The Germans with whom I talked were not too keen on a reunion
with East Germany. The West Germans have done a magnificent job of reconstruction while
the Russians in East Germany have done absolutely nothing. So if there mere a reunion
the demands of East Germany on the economy, the need for reconstruction and new
capital would set the whole economy back several years. It might lead to severe
inflation.
- 3 -

Hope to go to Captiva on February 3rd and stay there until the 18th when
Debby and I will go to Nassau to Join the PAA Directors on a ten day trip to Caracas,
Bogota, Canal Zone, Mexico City and Acapulco.
As ever,
H.M. B.
